items.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the length of a laboratory bench?
items.answer: A metre rule
items.markingKey: A metre rule (or tape) covers the length with millimetre resolution.

items.stem: Explain why a measurement of the time for one swing of a pendulum is less reliable than a measurement of the time for twenty swings.
items.answer: Reaction time (about 0.2 s) is the same for each timing, so for twenty swings it is a much smaller fraction of the total time; dividing by twenty gives a more accurate period.
items.markingKey: reaction time error similar for both [1]; smaller percentage of a longer time / divided by 20 [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by parallax error when reading a ruler, and how to avoid it.
items.answer: Reading the scale from an angle makes the object appear against the wrong mark; avoid it by looking perpendicular to the scale (eye directly in line with the mark).
items.markingKey: describes viewing at an angle [1]; eye perpendicular / in line with the mark [1] [2]

items.stem: Ines measures the total thickness of 430 sheets of paper in a ream as 4.6 cm. Calculate the thickness of one paper in mm.
items.markingKey: thickness = 46 mm / 430 = 0.107 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Kwame places a stack of 190 pages of a textbook (excluding the covers) against a ruler. The bottom of the stack is at the 1 cm mark and the top is at the 2.8 cm mark. Calculate the thickness of one page in millimetres.

In a practical exam, a candidate is given a child on a playground swing and a stopwatch reading to 0.01 s. (a) Explain why the stopwatch reading to 0.01 s does not make each timing accurate to 0.01 s. (b) Another student times only 1 oscillation and gets 1.27 s. Comment on this result.
items.answer: (a) Human reaction time (about 0.1–0.3 s) at start and stop is much larger than 0.01 s. (b) Less reliable: reaction-time error is a large fraction of a single period, so the value differs noticeably from the value from many oscillations.
items.markingKey: (a) reaction time [1]; much larger than resolution [1] [2] (b) compares with multiple-oscillation value [1]; reaction time large fraction [1] [2]

items.stem: How should the volume of water in a measuring cylinder be read?
options: At the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with the surface
At the top of the meniscus looking down from above
At any point, as long as the cylinder is tilted
At the highest point the water reaches on the glass
items.answer: At the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with the surface
items.markingKey: Read the bottom of the curved meniscus, eye level to avoid parallax error.

items.stem: Explain why a student should start a stopwatch as the pendulum passes through the centre of its swing rather than at the end of the swing.
items.answer: The bob moves fastest at the centre, so the moment it passes a fiducial mark there is easiest to judge; at the end it is momentarily still, so the exact moment is hard to judge.
items.markingKey: fastest at centre so passing moment clear [1]; end of swing is hard to judge [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why taking several readings of the same length and calculating the mean gives a more reliable result.
items.answer: Random errors make individual readings scatter above and below the true value; averaging reduces the effect of random errors and allows anomalous readings to be spotted.
items.markingKey: random errors / scatter [1]; averaging reduces their effect or anomalies identified [1] [2]

items.stem: A student uses a 30 cm ruler to measure the length of a corridor about 12 m long. Explain why this is a poor choice and suggest a better instrument.
items.answer: The ruler must be moved many times, so small errors add up at each move; a measuring tape or trundle wheel covers the length in one measurement.
items.markingKey: errors accumulate with repeated moves [1]; tape measure / trundle wheel [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the zero end of a worn ruler should not be used as the starting point for a measurement.
items.answer: The end may be damaged so 0 is not at the true zero (zero error); start from another mark such as 1.0 cm and subtract it.
items.markingKey: zero error from worn end [1]; start from another mark and subtract [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar times 30 complete oscillations of a ruler clamped to the bench and set vibrating and records 43.8 s. Work out the period of one oscillation.
items.markingKey: T = 43.8 / 30 = 1.46 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Lucas times 25 oscillations of a mass hanging from a spring bouncing up and down three times: 59.1 s, 58.7 s, 58.8 s. Calculate the mean time and hence the period.

Lucas wants the thickness of one slide. The bottom of a stack of 32 identical glass microscope slides is at the 2 cm mark of a ruler and the top is at 5.8 cm. (a) Calculate the thickness of one slide in mm. (b) Calculate the height of a stack of 96 of them in cm. (c) Explain why measuring a stack is better than measuring one slide.
items.answer: (a) 1.19 mm (b) 11.4 cm (c) one slide is too thin to measure precisely with a ruler; the reading error is shared over 32 items.
items.markingKey: (a) 5.8 − 2 = 3.8 cm; ÷ 32 = 1.19 mm [2] (b) 96 × 1.19 mm = 11.4 cm [1] (c) ruler resolution 1 mm too coarse for one item; error divided by number in stack [2] [5]

items.stem: Arjun investigates a child on a playground swing in a school laboratory in Auckland. (a) The time for 25 oscillations is 47.2 s. Calculate the period. (b) Another student times only 1 oscillation and gets 2.09 s. Comment on this result.
items.answer: (a) 1.89 s (b) Less reliable: reaction-time error is a large fraction of a single period, so the value differs noticeably from the value from many oscillations.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 47.2/25 = 1.89 s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.89 s with unit [1] [2] (b) compares with multiple-oscillation value [1]; reaction time large fraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas is asked to find the period of a child on a playground swing as accurately as possible. (a) The time for 20 oscillations is 17.8 s. Calculate the period. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant when comparing the periods of two pendulums of different lengths. (c) Another student times only 1 oscillation and gets 1.09 s. Comment on this result.
items.answer: (a) 0.89 s (b) Mass of bob and amplitude (starting angle) of swing; same timing method. (c) Less reliable: reaction-time error is a large fraction of a single period, so the value differs noticeably from the value from many oscillations.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 17.8/20 = 0.89 s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.89 s with unit [1] [2] (b) Mass of bob and amplitude (starting angle) of swing [1]; same timing method [1] [2] (c) compares with multiple-oscillation value [1]; reaction time large fraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Which equation defines density?
items.answer: density = mass ÷ volume
items.markingKey: ρ = m/V.

items.stem: A block of wood and a block of iron have the same mass. Explain which has the larger volume.
items.answer: The wood, because it is less dense; V = m/ρ, so for the same mass a smaller density means a larger volume.
items.markingKey: wood [1]; V = m/ρ with smaller ρ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a large ship made of steel floats although steel is denser than water.
items.answer: The ship is hollow and full of air, so its average density (total mass ÷ total volume enclosed) is less than that of water.
items.markingKey: hollow/air [1]; average density less than water [1] [2]

items.stem: A sample of aluminium shaped as a cuboid has a mass of 13.5 g and a volume of 5 cm³. Work out the density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 2.7 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = m/V = 13.5 / 5 = 2.7 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A small cork brick measures 5 cm × 6 cm × 1 cm and has a mass of 7.2 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 0.24 g/cm³

items.stem: A cuboid cut from glass measures 4 cm × 6 cm × 1 cm and has a mass of 0.06 kg. Calculate its density in kg/m³.
items.answer: 2500 kg/m³

items.stem: Kenji is given a cuboid of an unknown material measuring 3 cm × 2 cm × 1 cm. Its mass is 15 g. (a) State and explain whether it would float in water of density 1 g/cm³. (b) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) Sinks: its density is greater than 1 g/cm³. (b) Density unchanged at 2.5 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 15 = 120 g.
items.markingKey: (a) Sinks [1]; its density is greater than 1 g/cm³ [1] [2] (b) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel is given a cuboid of an unknown material measuring 2 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm. Its mass is 31.2 g. (a) Calculate its volume. (b) State and explain whether it would float in mercury of density 13.6 g/cm³. (c) Describe a different method to find its volume that would also work for an irregular shape.
items.answer: (a) 12 cm³ (b) Floats: its density is less than 13.6 g/cm³. (c) Lower it into a measuring cylinder of water (or displacement can) and find the rise in volume.
items.markingKey: (a) V = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 cm³: 12 cm³ [1] (b) Floats [1]; its density is less than 13.6 g/cm³ [1] [2] (c) displacement method [1]; volume = rise in level [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the SI unit of density?
items.answer: kg/m³
items.markingKey: Mass in kg divided by volume in m³ gives kg/m³ (g/cm³ is also used).

items.stem: The density of water is 1000 kg/m³. What is this in g/cm³?
items.answer: 1.0 g/cm³
items.markingKey: 1000 kg/m³ = 1.0 g/cm³ (divide by 1000).

items.stem: Describe how to find the density of an irregular stone.
items.answer: Find its mass on a balance; put water in a measuring cylinder, read the volume, lower the stone in and read again; volume = difference; density = mass ÷ volume.
items.markingKey: mass on balance [1]; displacement readings and subtract [1]; ρ = m/V [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe how to find the density of a liquid such as cooking oil.
items.answer: Weigh an empty measuring cylinder, add a measured volume of oil and weigh again; mass of oil = difference; density = mass ÷ volume.
items.markingKey: mass of empty cylinder and with oil [1]; volume read from cylinder [1]; ρ = m/V [1] [3]

items.stem: Ice floats on water, but solid wax sinks in liquid wax. Explain what this tells you about each substance when it freezes.
items.answer: Water expands on freezing so ice is less dense than water; wax contracts on freezing so solid wax is denser than liquid wax.
items.markingKey: ice less dense / water expands [1]; solid wax denser / contracts [1] [2]

items.stem: A student says a heavier object always has a greater density. Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Density depends on mass and volume; a heavy object may have a very large volume, e.g. a large log is heavier than a small steel bolt but less dense.
items.markingKey: density is mass per unit volume [1]; valid counter-example [1] [2]

items.stem: A small iron brick has a mass of 198 g and a volume of 25 cm³. What is the density in g/cm³?
items.answer: 7.9 g/cm³

items.stem: Lucas finds that a lump of marble has a mass of 13 g. It is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 40 cm³ to 45 cm³. Calculate the density of the object.
items.answer: 2.6 g/cm³
items.markingKey: V = 45 − 40 = 5 cm³; ρ = 13/5 = 2.6 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: 50 cm³ of olive oil has a mass of 46 g. Calculate the density of olive oil.
items.answer: 0.92 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = 46/50 = 0.92 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cuboid cut from brass has a mass of 85 g and a volume of 10 cm³. Determine the density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 8.5 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = m/V = 85 / 10 = 8.5 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Sipho finds the mass of a broken fragment of aluminium is 16.2 g. The water in a measuring cylinder reads 50 cm³ before and 56 cm³ after the object is fully submerged. Calculate the density in kg/m³.
items.answer: 2700 kg/m³

items.stem: Hana measures the density of a broken fragment of brass. Its mass is 51 g. The measuring cylinder reads 30 cm³ before and 36 cm³ after the object is submerged, but 4 cm³ of water splashed out as it was dropped in. (a) Calculate the density obtained if the splash is ignored. (b) Calculate the true density. (c) Suggest how to avoid this error.
items.answer: (a) 8.5 g/cm³ (b) 5.1 g/cm³ (c) lower the object gently on a thread / tilt the cylinder / use a displacement (Eureka) can.
items.markingKey: (a) 51/6 = 8.5 g/cm³ [1] (b) true V = 6 + 4 = 10 cm³ [1]; ρ = 5.1 g/cm³ [1] (c) sensible method [1] [4]

items.stem: A jeweller in Kathmandu is offered a block said to be granite. It measures 4 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm and has a mass of 43.2 g. (a) Calculate its volume. (b) Convert the density to kg/m³. (c) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) 16 cm³ (b) 2700 kg/m³ (c) Density unchanged at 2.7 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 43.2 = 346 g.
items.markingKey: (a) V = 4 × 2 × 2 = 16 cm³: 16 cm³ [1] (b) × 1000: 2700 kg/m³ [1] (c) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: A metal sample in a school laboratory is a cuboid 2 cm by 2.5 cm by 2 cm, with a mass of 26 g. (a) Calculate its density in g/cm³. (b) Describe a different method to find its volume that would also work for an irregular shape.
items.answer: (a) 2.6 g/cm³ (b) Lower it into a measuring cylinder of water (or displacement can) and find the rise in volume.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = m/V = 26/10 = 2.6 g/cm³ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.6 g/cm³ with unit [1] [2] (b) displacement method [1]; volume = rise in level [1] [2]

items.stem: A metal sample in a school laboratory is a cuboid 2 cm by 2.5 cm by 2 cm, with a mass of 105 g. (a) Calculate its volume. (b) Describe a different method to find its volume that would also work for an irregular shape. (c) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) 10 cm³ (b) Lower it into a measuring cylinder of water (or displacement can) and find the rise in volume. (c) Density unchanged at 10.5 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 105 = 840 g.
items.markingKey: (a) V = 2 × 2.5 × 2 = 10 cm³: 10 cm³ [1] (b) displacement method [1]; volume = rise in level [1] [2] (c) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity?
options: A vector has magnitude only; a scalar has direction only
A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only
A vector cannot be added; a scalar can
A scalar is always larger than a vector
items.answer: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only
items.markingKey: Vector: size and direction; scalar: size only.

items.stem: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track and returns to the start. Explain why the distance is 400 m but the displacement is zero.
items.answer: Distance is a scalar measuring the length of the path; displacement is a vector from start to finish, and start and finish are the same point.
items.markingKey: distance = path length (scalar) [1]; displacement = straight-line from start to finish, here zero (vector) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a car going round a roundabout at a steady 20 km/h has a changing velocity.
items.answer: Velocity is a vector; the direction of motion is changing, so the velocity changes even though the speed is constant.
items.markingKey: velocity has direction [1]; direction changes [1] [2]

items.stem: A drone flies at 10 m/s due west while a wind blows it due south at 6 m/s. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant velocity.
items.markingKey: R = √(10² + 6²) = 11.7 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A boat heads straight across a river at 12 m/s while the current flows downstream at 16 m/s. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant velocity and the angle it makes with the 12 m/s vector.

Two dogs pull on a toy with leads attached to the same point. The forces are 40 N and 30 N and the angle between them is 90°. (a) Using a scale of 1 cm to 10 N, describe how to draw a scale diagram to find the resultant. (b) Explain why the resultant is smaller than the sum of the two forces.
items.answer: (a) Draw a 4 cm arrow, then from its tip a 3 cm arrow at 90° to it (angle between vectors 90°); join start to finish and measure. (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions.
items.markingKey: (a) arrow lengths correct for scale [1]; tip-to-tail at correct angle [1]; measure closing side [1] [3] (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions [1]

items.stem: Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act on an object in opposite directions. What is the resultant force?
options: 2 N in the direction of the 3 N force
2 N in the direction of the 5 N force
items.answer: 2 N in the direction of the 5 N force
items.markingKey: Opposite directions: subtract; 5 − 3 = 2 N towards the larger force.

items.stem: Which of these is a vector quantity: volume, force, density, time? Give a reason.
items.answer: Force: it has direction as well as magnitude.
items.markingKey: correct choice [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why two forces of 4 N and 7 N cannot have a resultant of 12 N.
items.answer: The largest resultant is when they act in the same direction: 4 + 7 = 11 N; any other angle gives less.
items.markingKey: maximum is sum 11 N [1]; so 12 N impossible [1] [2]

items.stem: A student says "temperature is a vector because it can be negative". Explain why the student is wrong.
items.answer: A negative temperature only means below zero on the scale; it has no direction in space, so it is a scalar.
items.markingKey: negative sign is not a direction [1]; temperature has magnitude only [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how to use a scale drawing to find the resultant of two forces acting at 60° to each other.
items.answer: Choose a scale; draw one force as an arrow of the right length, then draw the second from its tip at the correct angle; the line from the start to the final tip is the resultant: measure its length and angle.
items.markingKey: scale chosen [1]; tip-to-tail at correct angle [1]; measure length and direction of closing side [1] [3]

items.stem: Two forces act on a boat being rowed against the wind along the same line in opposite directions: 150 N to the right and 80 N to the left. Determine the resultant force (to the right).
items.markingKey: R = 150 − 80 = 70 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Tariq pulls a sledge with a force of 30 N forwards while Samuel pulls it sideways with 40 N, at right angles. Work out the magnitude of the resultant force.
items.markingKey: R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Forces act along a straight line on a car on a straight road: 400 N and 50 N to the right, and 180 N to the left. Calculate the resultant force, giving its direction, and state whether the forces are balanced.
items.answer: 270 N to the right; not balanced.
items.markingKey: R = 400 + 50 − 180 [1] = 270 N [1]; direction / balanced statement [1] [3]

items.stem: Two cables hold a load at a construction site in Dubai. The forces are 30 N and 40 N and the angle between them is 90°. (a) Using a scale of 1 cm to 10 N, describe how to draw a scale diagram to find the resultant. (b) Explain why the resultant is smaller than the sum of the two forces.
items.answer: (a) Draw a 3 cm arrow, then from its tip a 4 cm arrow at 90° to it (angle between vectors 90°); join start to finish and measure. (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions.
items.markingKey: (a) arrow lengths correct for scale [1]; tip-to-tail at correct angle [1]; measure closing side [1] [3] (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions [1]

items.stem: Two cables hold a load at a construction site in Muscat. The forces are 45 N and 20 N and the angle between them is 90°. (a) State the magnitude of the resultant (from an accurate drawing). (b) Explain why the resultant is smaller than the sum of the two forces. (c) State how the resultant changes if the angle between the forces is reduced.
items.answer: (a) about 49 N (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions. (c) It increases, towards a maximum of the sum when the angle is 0°.
items.markingKey: (a) 49.2 N (accept ±1 N) [1]; about 49 N [1] [2] (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions [1] (c) increases [1]; max = sum at 0° [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the SI unit of time?
items.answer: second (s)
items.markingKey: The SI base unit of time is the second.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student uses a 30 cm ruler to measure the length of a corridor about 12 m long. Explain why this is a poor choice and suggest a better instrument. (b) Explain why taking several readings of the same length and calculating the mean gives a more reliable result.
items.answer: (a) The ruler must be moved many times, so small errors add up at each move; a measuring tape or trundle wheel covers the length in one measurement. (b) Random errors make individual readings scatter above and below the true value; averaging reduces the effect of random errors and allows anomalous readings to be spotted.
items.markingKey: (a) errors accumulate with repeated moves [1]; tape measure / trundle wheel [1] [2] (b) random errors / scatter [1]; averaging reduces their effect or anomalies identified [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why taking several readings of the same length and calculating the mean gives a more reliable result. (b) A student uses a 30 cm ruler to measure the length of a corridor about 12 m long. Explain why this is a poor choice and suggest a better instrument.
items.answer: (a) Random errors make individual readings scatter above and below the true value; averaging reduces the effect of random errors and allows anomalous readings to be spotted. (b) The ruler must be moved many times, so small errors add up at each move; a measuring tape or trundle wheel covers the length in one measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) random errors / scatter [1]; averaging reduces their effect or anomalies identified [1] [2] (b) errors accumulate with repeated moves [1]; tape measure / trundle wheel [1] [2]

items.stem: A measuring cylinder contains 30 cm³ of water. A small stone is lowered in and the water level rises to 39 cm³. Determine the volume of the object.
items.answer: 9 cm³
items.markingKey: V = 39 − 30 = 9 cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A measuring cylinder contains 50 cm³ of water. When a brass key is lowered in, the reading rises to 54 cm³. State the volume of the object in cm³ and in m³, and state one precaution when taking the readings.
items.answer: 4 cm³ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³; read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level / lower gently so no water splashes out.

items.stem: In a practical exam, a candidate is given a pendulum made from a metal bob on a string and a stopwatch reading to 0.01 s. (a) Explain why the stopwatch reading to 0.01 s does not make each timing accurate to 0.01 s. (b) Another student times only 1 oscillation and gets 2.14 s. Comment on this result.
items.answer: (a) Human reaction time (about 0.1–0.3 s) at start and stop is much larger than 0.01 s. (b) Less reliable: reaction-time error is a large fraction of a single period, so the value differs noticeably from the value from many oscillations.
items.markingKey: (a) reaction time [1]; much larger than resolution [1] [2] (b) compares with multiple-oscillation value [1]; reaction time large fraction [1] [2]

items.stem: An object will float on water if …
options: its density is greater than that of water
its volume is greater than that of the water
its mass is less than 1 kg
its density is less than the density of water
items.answer: its density is less than the density of water
items.markingKey: Objects less dense than the liquid float; denser objects sink.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A block of wood and a block of iron have the same mass. Explain which has the larger volume. (b) Ice floats on water, but solid wax sinks in liquid wax. Explain what this tells you about each substance when it freezes.
items.answer: (a) The wood, because it is less dense; V = m/ρ, so for the same mass a smaller density means a larger volume. (b) Water expands on freezing so ice is less dense than water; wax contracts on freezing so solid wax is denser than liquid wax.
items.markingKey: (a) wood [1]; V = m/ρ with smaller ρ [1] [2] (b) ice less dense / water expands [1]; solid wax denser / contracts [1] [2]

items.stem: A solid piece of aluminium (density 2700 kg/m³) is placed in glycerol (density 1260 kg/m³). Predict whether it floats or sinks and explain your answer.
items.answer: It sinks, because its density is greater than the density of the glycerol.
items.markingKey: correct prediction [1]; comparison of densities [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf finds that an irregular piece of glass has a mass of 37.5 g. It is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 60 cm³ to 75 cm³. Calculate the density of the object.
items.answer: 2.5 g/cm³
items.markingKey: V = 75 − 60 = 15 cm³; ρ = 37.5/15 = 2.5 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: 150 cm³ of mercury has a mass of 2040 g. Work out the density of mercury.
items.answer: 13.6 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = 2040/150 = 13.6 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cuboid cut from pine wood has a mass of 37.5 g and a volume of 75 cm³. Work out the density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 0.5 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = m/V = 37.5 / 75 = 0.5 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A jeweller in Kuala Lumpur is offered a block said to be gold. It measures 4 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm and has a mass of 309 g. (a) State and explain whether it would float in ethanol of density 0.79 g/cm³. (b) Describe a different method to find its volume that would also work for an irregular shape.
items.answer: (a) Sinks: its density is greater than 0.79 g/cm³. (b) Lower it into a measuring cylinder of water (or displacement can) and find the rise in volume.
items.markingKey: (a) Sinks [1]; its density is greater than 0.79 g/cm³ [1] [2] (b) displacement method [1]; volume = rise in level [1] [2]

items.stem: A jeweller in Manila is offered a block said to be iron. It measures 3 cm × 5 cm × 2 cm and has a mass of 237 g. (a) Convert the density to kg/m³. (b) State and explain whether it would float in mercury of density 13.6 g/cm³. (c) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) 7900 kg/m³ (b) Floats: its density is less than 13.6 g/cm³. (c) Density unchanged at 7.9 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 237 = 1900 g.
items.markingKey: (a) × 1000: 7900 kg/m³ [1] (b) Floats [1]; its density is less than 13.6 g/cm³ [1] [2] (c) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity? (b) Which method can be used to find the resultant of two forces at an angle other than 90°?
items.answer: (a) A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only (b) A scale drawing (parallelogram or triangle of vectors)
items.markingKey: (a) Vector: size and direction; scalar: size only. (b) Draw the vectors to scale, tip to tail, and measure the resultant.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track and returns to the start. Explain why the distance is 400 m but the displacement is zero. (b) Explain why a car going round a roundabout at a steady 20 km/h has a changing velocity.
items.answer: (a) Distance is a scalar measuring the length of the path; displacement is a vector from start to finish, and start and finish are the same point. (b) Velocity is a vector; the direction of motion is changing, so the velocity changes even though the speed is constant.
items.markingKey: (a) distance = path length (scalar) [1]; displacement = straight-line from start to finish, here zero (vector) [1] [2] (b) velocity has direction [1]; direction changes [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student says "temperature is a vector because it can be negative". Explain why the student is wrong. (b) A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track and returns to the start. Explain why the distance is 400 m but the displacement is zero.
items.answer: (a) A negative temperature only means below zero on the scale; it has no direction in space, so it is a scalar. (b) Distance is a scalar measuring the length of the path; displacement is a vector from start to finish, and start and finish are the same point.
items.markingKey: (a) negative sign is not a direction [1]; temperature has magnitude only [1] [2] (b) distance = path length (scalar) [1]; displacement = straight-line from start to finish, here zero (vector) [1] [2]

items.stem: Two forces act on a boat being rowed against the wind along the same line in opposite directions: 480 N to the right and 160 N to the left. Work out the resultant force (to the right).
items.markingKey: R = 480 − 160 = 320 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Mateo pulls a sledge with a force of 8 N forwards while Sipho pulls it sideways with 15 N, at right angles. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force and the angle it makes with the 8 N vector.

Two ropes pull a stuck car out of mud. The forces are 35 N and 35 N and the angle between them is 90°. (a) Using a scale of 1 cm to 5 N, describe how to draw a scale diagram to find the resultant. (b) Explain why the resultant is smaller than the sum of the two forces. (c) State how the resultant changes if the angle between the forces is reduced.
items.answer: (a) Draw a 7 cm arrow, then from its tip a 7 cm arrow at 90° to it (angle between vectors 90°); join start to finish and measure. (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions. (c) It increases, towards a maximum of the sum when the angle is 0°.
items.markingKey: (a) arrow lengths correct for scale [1]; tip-to-tail at correct angle [1]; measure closing side [1] [3] (b) The forces are not in the same direction, so part of each force acts in different directions [1] (c) increases [1]; max = sum at 0° [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why taking several readings of the same length and calculating the mean gives a more reliable result. (b) Explain why a student should start a stopwatch as the pendulum passes through the centre of its swing rather than at the end of the swing.
items.answer: (a) Random errors make individual readings scatter above and below the true value; averaging reduces the effect of random errors and allows anomalous readings to be spotted. (b) The bob moves fastest at the centre, so the moment it passes a fiducial mark there is easiest to judge; at the end it is momentarily still, so the exact moment is hard to judge.
items.markingKey: (a) random errors / scatter [1]; averaging reduces their effect or anomalies identified [1] [2] (b) fastest at centre so passing moment clear [1]; end of swing is hard to judge [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a measurement of the time for one swing of a pendulum is less reliable than a measurement of the time for twenty swings. (b) Explain why taking several readings of the same length and calculating the mean gives a more reliable result.
items.answer: (a) Reaction time (about 0.2 s) is the same for each timing, so for twenty swings it is a much smaller fraction of the total time; dividing by twenty gives a more accurate period. (b) Random errors make individual readings scatter above and below the true value; averaging reduces the effect of random errors and allows anomalous readings to be spotted.
items.markingKey: (a) reaction time error similar for both [1]; smaller percentage of a longer time / divided by 20 [1] [2] (b) random errors / scatter [1]; averaging reduces their effect or anomalies identified [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara measures the total thickness of 470 sheets of paper in a ream as 4.4 cm. Work out the thickness of one paper in mm.
items.markingKey: thickness = 44 mm / 470 = 0.0936 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Mateo places a stack of 37 identical CDs in a spindle against a ruler. The bottom of the stack is at the 0.5 cm mark and the top is at the 4.8 cm mark. Calculate the thickness of one CD in millimetres.

Lina investigates a metronome arm in a school laboratory in Seoul. (a) Describe how the student should use a fiducial marker. (b) Suggest why the number of oscillations should not be counted as "1" when the timer is started.
items.answer: (a) Place a marker (pin or line) at the centre of the swing and start/stop timing as the bob passes it in the same direction. (b) Counting must start from zero at the start so that the number of complete oscillations is correct; starting at 1 gives one too many.
items.markingKey: (a) marker at centre/rest position [1]; time as bob passes it in same direction [1] [2] (b) count 0 at start [1]; otherwise one oscillation too many [1] [2]

items.stem: Which method is used to find the volume of an irregularly shaped stone?
options: Measuring its length, width and height
Timing how long it takes to sink
Displacement of water in a measuring cylinder
items.answer: Displacement of water in a measuring cylinder
items.markingKey: The rise in water level equals the volume of the stone.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student says a heavier object always has a greater density. Explain why this is wrong. (b) Ice floats on water, but solid wax sinks in liquid wax. Explain what this tells you about each substance when it freezes.
items.answer: (a) Density depends on mass and volume; a heavy object may have a very large volume, e.g. a large log is heavier than a small steel bolt but less dense. (b) Water expands on freezing so ice is less dense than water; wax contracts on freezing so solid wax is denser than liquid wax.
items.markingKey: (a) density is mass per unit volume [1]; valid counter-example [1] [2] (b) ice less dense / water expands [1]; solid wax denser / contracts [1] [2]

items.stem: A solid piece of marble (density 2600 kg/m³) is placed in water (density 1000 kg/m³). Predict whether it floats or sinks and explain your answer.
items.answer: It sinks, because its density is greater than the density of the water.
items.markingKey: correct prediction [1]; comparison of densities [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah finds that an irregular piece of zinc has a mass of 142 g. It is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 50 cm³ to 70 cm³. Work out the density of the object.
items.answer: 7.1 g/cm³
items.markingKey: V = 70 − 50 = 20 cm³; ρ = 142/20 = 7.1 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: 100 cm³ of paraffin has a mass of 80 g. Calculate the density of paraffin.
items.answer: 0.8 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = 80/100 = 0.8 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample of lead shaped as a cuboid has a mass of 113 g and a volume of 10 cm³. Determine the density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 11.3 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = m/V = 113 / 10 = 11.3 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A jeweller in Seoul is offered a block said to be silver. It measures 2 cm × 5 cm × 1 cm and has a mass of 105 g. (a) State and explain whether it would float in ethanol of density 0.79 g/cm³. (b) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) Sinks: its density is greater than 0.79 g/cm³. (b) Density unchanged at 10.5 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 105 = 840 g.
items.markingKey: (a) Sinks [1]; its density is greater than 0.79 g/cm³ [1] [2] (b) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace is given a cuboid of an unknown material measuring 3 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm. Its mass is 160 g. (a) Calculate its density in g/cm³. (b) Convert the density to kg/m³. (c) State and explain whether it would float in milk of density 1.03 g/cm³.
items.answer: (a) 8.9 g/cm³ (b) 8900 kg/m³ (c) Sinks: its density is greater than 1.03 g/cm³.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = m/V = 160/18 = 8.9 g/cm³ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.9 g/cm³ with unit [1] [2] (b) × 1000: 8900 kg/m³ [1] (c) Sinks [1]; its density is greater than 1.03 g/cm³ [1] [2]
